displaced_geometry.label: Displaced geometry
displaced_geometry.measures: Rows whose centroid falls outside the parent they claim, and which overlap that parent by less than half their own area.
displaced_geometry.reading: Treat as background noise unless a specific jurisdiction is misbehaving. The scan caps this check per run, so the number is a ceiling and not a count — read it as "at least this many".
displaced_geometry.remedy: Reparent when a specific row is wrong; otherwise leave it.
displaced_geometry.why: A row sitting outside its parent usually means the source drew the two boundaries against different coastlines or vintages. Genuine mis-parenting shows up here too, but at world scale most of it is geographic noise.
dual_coverage.label: Dual coverage
dual_coverage.measures: A country whose representative surface point is also covered by another country's tree.
dual_coverage.reading: Informational by design. A non-zero count is the expected state of the world, not a problem to drive to zero.
dual_coverage.remedy: Accept the flag; prune a side only on a deliberate decision about which claim this instance recognises.
dual_coverage.why: Two nations claim the same ground. The data records both because the dispute is real, and the platform is built to let both coexist in one game space rather than pick a winner.
mis_anchored_cluster.label: Mis-anchored clusters
mis_anchored_cluster.measures: A parent holding three or more children that each sit almost entirely outside it — less than 5% overlap.
mis_anchored_cluster.reading: Small and stable. Most entries are real: archipelagos and overseas territories, faithfully recorded.
mis_anchored_cluster.remedy: Synthesize an anchor when the group deserves its own parent; accept when the arrangement is the real one.
mis_anchored_cluster.why: This is the grouped form of displaced geometry: not one stray row but a whole set anchored to the wrong place. In practice it mostly surfaces the administrative legacy of colonial systems — overseas departments and island groups administered from a mainland parent.
national_delta_gt5.label: Attribution delta
national_delta_gt5.measures: A parent whose own population differs from the sum of its children's by more than 5%.
national_delta_gt5.reading: A map-health trend line, not a defect list. It was invaluable for diagnosing district-drawing problems; day to day, watch whether it grows.
national_delta_gt5.remedy: None automatic — it points at which layer to look at.
national_delta_gt5.why: Each level is attributed independently from the raster, so parent and children should land on nearly the same total. A gap means the child layer overlaps itself or leaves holes relative to the parent — the distortion that shows up later as uneven district populations.
nature.informational.hint: A statistic to watch, not a defect to clear.
nature.structural.hint: The tree itself is wrong — act on this.
orphaned_rows.label: Orphaned rows
orphaned_rows.measures: Live jurisdictions with no living parent — either no parent at all, or one that has been removed.
orphaned_rows.reading: Expect zero. Any non-zero count is worth acting on, and the count understates it: a detached parent takes its whole subtree with it.
orphaned_rows.remedy: Reparent — though the right answer is sometimes that the row is genuinely top-level and should become an L1 of its own.
orphaned_rows.why: Anything that walks the tree down from Earth — districting, apportionment, population rollups — simply cannot see a detached row. It is the one check here that describes a defect rather than the world.
raster_coverage.label: Raster coverage
raster_coverage.measures: Countries with no population raster tiles at all, or with tiles but a stored population under half of what the raster holds for that footprint.
raster_coverage.reading: Each entry is a real gap worth knowing about. "No tiles" is a limitation of the population source, not something a rescan will fix.
raster_coverage.remedy: Recompute population where tiles exist; accept where the source genuinely has no coverage.
raster_coverage.why: Population is the input to the seat law — the chamber size is the cube root of it. A country the raster does not cover cannot be sized, and one counted far under its raster will be under-represented.
same_space_chain.label: Same-space chains
same_space_chain.measures: A parent whose single child covers the identical footprint — byte-identical geometry, or areas within 2% of each other with a negligible symmetric difference. Consecutive pairs chain into runs.
same_space_chain.reading: Concentrated by country rather than spread evenly — a national statistics office either subdivides that layer or it does not. Large counts in one country are a property of that source, not damage.
same_space_chain.remedy: Merge the chain: the topmost row survives as the playable jurisdiction and inherits the lower twin's children.
same_space_chain.why: The source release recorded one place twice at two administrative levels. The two rows are the same ground, so one of them is a pass-through link rather than a distinct place to govern.
stray_synthetic.label: Stray synthetics
stray_synthetic.measures: Country rows that are synthesized placeholders even though the source dataset ships a real ADM0 boundary file for that country.
stray_synthetic.reading: Expect zero. Any entry is worth acting on immediately — the row it names is standing in for real data that exists on disk.
stray_synthetic.remedy: Re-run the boundary import scoped to that country: the importer upgrades the placeholder in place with the shipped geometry, then re-attribution restores its population.
stray_synthetic.why: A placeholder country carries derived geometry and population instead of the imported ones — every rollup, seat count and map above it inherits the error. The importer synthesizes a country row only when the dataset truly ships none (Puerto Rico); one appearing where a file exists means an import race replaced real data, the defect the Philippines certification run caught.
